title: Two piggy banks
scenario: Two piggy banks, A and B. Add n coins to A only, then print both counts.

intro.job: Two piggy banks, A and B. Add n coins to A only, then print both counts.

idea.rule: Class attributes are the shared whiteboard; self. attributes are each bank's own label — write on the wrong one and everyone sees it.
idea.detail: Anything set directly in the class body (coins = 0) belongs to the class — every bank reads the same one. self.coins = 0 inside __init__ runs once per new bank and gives THAT bank its own coins. Inside a method, self.coins means 'this bank's coins'; Piggy.coins means 'the shared one'.

    def __init__(self):
        self.coins = 0
    def add(self, n):
        self.coins += n

b = Piggy()

model_restatement: Make two piggy banks, add coins to bank A only, and show both counts — B should still be 0.

clarify.question: What does a piggy bank start with?
What should I print?
clarify.answer: Both counts, as (A's coins, B's coins).

clarify_fallback: Good question — assume the simple case.

why_line: coins lives on the class and add changes Piggy.coins — there's only one count, shared by every bank, so B reads the 5 too.

explain.rule: Piggy.coins is the whiteboard in the kitchen: write 5 on it for bank A, and bank B — reading the same board — says 5 as well.
explain.bridge: So where should each bank keep its own count?

fix.rule: self.coins = 0 in __init__ gives each new bank its own label; self.coins += n writes only on this bank's label.

walk.gloss: Make bank A — __init__ gives it its own coins of 0.
Make bank B — its own coins of 0 too.
Add n to A's coins only.
